name: Lithium-ion
plain: A rechargeable battery at 3.6 to 3.7 volts, the kind used in laptops, tools and vehicles. It needs a charger made for it and does not work in devices built for 1.5-volt batteries.
cathode: Lithium metal oxide: cobalt (LCO), nickel manganese cobalt (NMC), nickel cobalt aluminum (NCA) or manganese (LMO)
electrolyte: Lithium hexafluorophosphate in a mixture of organic carbonates
self_discharge: 1.5 to 2% per month as typically stated by manufacturers (Wikipedia)
summary: Lithium-ion batteries shuttle lithium ions between a graphite anode and a lithium metal oxide cathode, giving 3.6 to 3.7V nominal and a 4.2V full charge. The family includes LCO, NMC, NCA and LMO cathodes and the 18650 and 21700 batteries used in laptops, tools and vehicles.
body:
## How it works

Every commercial lithium-ion battery uses intercalation compounds: lithium ions move into and out of the crystal structure of both electrodes rather than plating as metal. The negative electrode is usually graphite, sometimes with silicon added for capacity. The electrolyte is usually lithium hexafluorophosphate dissolved in a mixture of organic carbonates. Energizer notes that lithium-ion batteries do not contain metallic lithium, which separates them from single-use lithium batteries. The positive electrode defines the subtype. Battery University's summary lists lithium cobalt oxide (LCO) at 3.60V nominal and 150 to 200Wh/kg, lithium manganese oxide (LMO) at 3.70V and 100 to 150Wh/kg, nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) at 3.60 to 3.70V and 150 to 220Wh/kg, and nickel cobalt aluminum (NCA) at 3.60V and 200 to 260Wh/kg. Lithium iron phosphate and lithium titanate batteries, also lithium-ion, have separate entries here.

## Discharge behavior

Voltage slopes from 4.2V at full charge through a nominal 3.6 to 3.7V. Panasonic's NCR18650B, an 18650 battery, is specified at 3.6V nominal, charged by constant current then constant voltage to 4.20V, and discharged to 2.50V; it is rated for discharge from −20 to 60°C, charge from 0 to 45°C and storage from −20 to 50°C, at 243Wh/kg and 676Wh/L. Battery University gives 3.00V as the full-discharge point for LCO, LMO, NMC and NCA and 2.50V as the minimum. Wikipedia notes that charging above 45°C degrades performance and that charging between 0 and 5°C needs reduced current. Self-discharge is typically 1.5 to 2% per month. Battery University lists ideal cycle life from 300 to 700 cycles for LMO up to 1,000 to 2,000 for NMC.

## Uses

Phones, laptops, cameras, power tools, e-bikes, medical devices and electric vehicles, according to Battery University's application list. IEC 61960-3 designates batteries by negative electrode (I for carbon), positive electrode (C cobalt, N nickel, M manganese) and shape (R cylindrical, P prismatic), followed by diameter and height in millimeters, as in ICR19/66. The five-digit names in common use, such as 18650 (18mm by 65.0mm), follow the IEC 60086 round-battery size pattern instead.

## History

Stanley Whittingham conceived intercalation electrodes in the 1970s and built a rechargeable battery with a titanium disulfide cathode. John Goodenough added the lithium cobalt oxide cathode in 1980. Akira Yoshino developed the first prototype of the modern battery, with a carbonaceous anode, in 1985, and a Sony and Asahi Kasei team commercialized it in 1991. Whittingham, Goodenough and Yoshino shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. From 1991 to 2018, energy density more than tripled.

## Status

Current.
strengths: High specific energy: 100 to 260Wh/kg across common subtypes (Battery University)
Low self-discharge for a rechargeable: 1.5 to 2% per month
limitations: Needs charge control to 4.2V and discharge protection below about 2.5V
Degradation increases with storage or use at high or low temperature (Wikipedia)
safety: Thermal runaway can begin near 150°C for LCO and NCA batteries (Battery University)
Charging too fast or too cold can plate lithium metal on the anode; the dendrites can pierce the separator and short the battery internally (Wikipedia)
A short circuit can lead to overheating, explosion and fire (Wikipedia)
